S&P projects Meta's leverage will hit 1.3x by 2028, past the 1.0x downgrade threshold, with the shortfall funded "entirely with debt."

On October 30, 2026, S&P Global Ratings maintained Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) at AA- and revised its outlook from stable to negative. S&P pointed to uncertainty about elevated capital spending and negative free cash flow, writing: "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers."

Fritz Jorgensen / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

The shares fell 1.53% to close at $614.99, a market value of $1.36 trillion, and traded at $614.43 after hours. That close sits 1.6% below the $625 price Meta charged for new stock on October 26.

October was already Meta's worst month in four years, down 15.2% from a $725.18 close, including a 6.98% drop on October 22. The ad business is growing fast, but the AI bill is growing faster, and shareholders now cover part of it.

What S&P Kept and What It Flagged

S&P left the rating unchanged, and AA- remains among the highest credit ratings in tech, while a negative outlook is a formal warning that a downgrade becomes possible if the agency's forecast holds.

S&P wrote that "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years." Meta's payback has to come through ads, engagement, and products still being built, because its model relies on its own apps rather than cloud-style computing rentals to outside customers.

Spokesperson Kamran Mumtaz replied, "We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," adding, "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."

StreetInsider reported that the Gulf South utility raised its quarterly dividend by 6.3%, setting the new payout at $0.68 per share, payable December 1, for an annual total of $2.72. That is a moderate payout ratio for a regulated utility that also has to keep cash for construction. In 2025, adjusted EPS was $3.91, which landed in the top half of guidance.

title: Zuckerberg Says Meta’s “Core Business Is Strong.” S&P Still Cut Its Outlook to Negative
detail:
Zuckerberg Says Meta’s “Core Business Is Strong.” S&P Still Cut Its Outlook to Negative

SPGI
META

Trading disclosure
Zuckerberg Says Meta's "Core Business Is Strong." S&P Still Cut Its Outlook to Negative ©Marcel Pirosca and Peopleimages.com - YuriArcurs via Canva
Key Takeaways

S&P revised Meta's outlook to negative and kept its AA- rating, forecasting free operating cash flow deficits of $22 billion in 2026 and $71 billion in 2027.

Third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, but capex of $34.9 billion outran operating cash flow, leaving free cash flow at negative $2.12 billion.

Meta plans a record $97.5 billion equity raise and created a new non-voting share class, with Nvidia investing $3 billion.

The fourth-quarter report, expected around January 27, needs a 2027 capex guide well below S&P's $225 billion forecast.

Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) spent most of its public life printing cash. On Friday, S&P Global revised its outlook on Meta to negative, keeping the AA- rating but flagging uncertainty over how long capex stays elevated and free cash flow stays negative.

The stock slipped 1.5% to $615, leaving it 21% below its 52-week high of $780.

Meta's suppliers have a stake in how this plays out. Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) agreed to invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering, and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) advanced a partnership this week that covers 6 gigawatts of its GPUs. So the chipmakers are now helping fund demand for their own chips.

The ad business looks fine. What's uncertain is how much more it costs to keep Muse, Meta's AI agent, growing.

S&P puts numbers on the deficit

S&P now forecasts Meta's capex at:

$140 billion in 2026

More than $225 billion in 2027

$252 billion in 2028

On that path, it sees free operating cash flow deficits of $22 billion in 2026 and $71 billion in 2027. It also expects Meta to fund the 2028 shortfall entirely with debt.

Meta is raising money ahead of that. It plans a record $97.5 billion equity raise, including an upsized $37.5 billion underwritten offering, and it created a new non-voting share class to do it. Non-cancelable contractual commitments reached $454.5 billion at the end of September.

How does the Street's free cash flow forecast compare?

Meta Platforms (META): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023–2028 (TIKR)

S&P's view is that the bottom is still ahead, so watch whether consensus drifts toward it.

The ad machine is still humming

Revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion in the third quarter. Ad impressions grew 10% and average price per ad rose 14%, so Meta sold more ads and charged more for each one.

Mark Zuckerberg said in the results release that "the core business is strong, and we're seeing velocity across the board." Fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $73 billion to $76 billion landed in line with consensus.

Reported EPS of $3.83 includes a $9.89 billion charge tied to the multistate attorneys general settlement. Excluding it, EPS was $7.40. Operating income still fell 37% to $12.99 billion as infrastructure, legal and third-party AI token costs all climbed.
